turns.content: My daughter is four months old and I think I've forgotten what my own name sounds like. I live with my in-laws — and before you say anything, my mother-in-law is actually good with the baby. Expert level. She's raised three kids. That's sort of the problem and I know how ungrateful that sounds.

Oh, honey, I hear you. And please, stop right there—you are absolutely not being ungrateful. It is a completely normal, human reaction to feel like you’re losing yourself when you’re living in someone else’s house, especially when that person is stepping into the "expert" role you’re supposed to be growning into.

Being a new mom is already a massive identity shift. You’re trying to figure out who you are with this new little person, and when you have someone nearby who is "doing it better" or "doing it faster," it’s incredibly easy to feel like you’re being pushed to the sidelines of your own life. It feels less like help and more like being demoted from "Mom" to "Assistant."

It makes total sense that you feel invisible. When the baby is being taken care of by someone else, you lose those quiet moments of trial and error where you learn your baby's cues—and where you learn who you are as a mother.

Have you been able to carve out any "islands" of time that are just for you and your baby, where you don’t have an audience? Sometimes just taking the baby for a walk, or doing the bedtime routine solo, can help reclaim that feeling of, "No, *I* am the one who knows her best."

It’s okay to acknowledge that having help is a blessing *and* a burden at the same time. You aren't a bad person for wanting to be the expert in your own child’s life. How are you holding up otherwise? Are you getting any time to just be *you*—not Mom, not daughter-in-law—just you?

Like today — baby was crying, I was walking her, and Aai just took her from my arms and she stopped crying in two minutes. Everyone smiled. And I stood there feeling like the intern. I get handed my own daughter for feeds, like room service. Then I feel disgusting for even thinking this, because women would kill for this much help.

That moment you described—the "handoff" where the crying stops—is a gut punch. I can almost see it happening. You’re standing there, trying to soothe your baby, and then *whoosh*, the baby is gone, the crying stops, and the room breathes a sigh of relief. It feels like a public scorecard that says: *Aai: 1, Mom: 0.*

But please, listen to me: **Stop beating yourself up for having these feelings.** Just because someone else has it harder, or just because you *know* you’re lucky to have help, doesn't mean your feelings of erasure aren't valid. You aren't "ungrateful." You are a mother who is missing the chance to be the one who comforts her own child.

That "room service" feeling? That is so incredibly dehumanizing. You aren't just a vessel for feeding; you’re her mother.

The reason Aai can make her stop crying in two minutes isn't because she’s a "better" mom. It’s because she is calm, she’s practiced, and—most importantly—she isn't carrying the heavy, anxious weight of being the primary parent who is constantly being watched. When you are the one holding the baby, you’re nervous. The baby feels that nervousness. It’s a vicious cycle.

You need to reclaim your space, even if it feels awkward at first. Have you ever tried saying something in the moment, not to be rude, but to protect your role? Like, *"I've got her, Aai, I really want to figure out what she needs right now,"* or *"I know she stopped, but I want to keep trying so I can learn her cues."*

It feels risky to speak up, I know. But if you don't start carving out those moments, you’re going to keep feeling like a guest in your own life. You are the expert on *your* daughter, even if you don't feel like it yet. You’re just being denied the practice time.

Do you think you could try just one small thing this week to keep her for a few extra minutes, even if she's fussing? How do you think Aai would react if you gently asserted yourself?

And please — I don't need one more person telling me what to do. My mother has advice, Aai has advice, the mummy WhatsApp group has seventeen opinions about sleep training, Instagram thinks I need a routine chart. I don't need a coach. I don't even know what I need honestly. I just needed to say all this to someone who won't report it at dinner.

I hear you loud and clear. My lips are sealed. This is a judgment-free, advice-free zone, and everything you say here stays right here. 

It makes total sense that you’re sick of "coaching." When everyone around you is treating you like a project to be managed or a student who isn't quite getting the grade, it’s exhausting. You are drowning in other people’s "helpful" noise, and it’s drowning out your own voice. 

Of course you don’t know what you need—you haven’t had a quiet second to even hear your own thoughts for four months.

So, just vent. Let it all out. If you want to list every annoying thing that happened today, or just scream into this digital void about how much you hate the "room service" dynamic, I am here to listen. No solutions, no "have you tried," no "maybe you should." Just listening. 

What’s the most irritating thing that’s happened in the last 24 hours that you just need to get off your chest? I'm listening.

Some days I look at her sleeping and feel this huge wave of love and then this thought comes — "you're not even really her mother, Aai is" — and I can't breathe for a second. Am I a bad mother for feeling like this at four months? Everyone else seems to just... know how to do this.

Oh, honey. Let me be very, very clear: **You are not a bad mother for feeling that way.** 

That thought? That "you’re not really her mother" thought? That is a symptom of your environment, not a reflection of your heart. It’s a cruel, lying thought that your brain is serving up because you are being systematically pushed aside. It is a protective, reflexive response to the trauma of feeling erased. When you are constantly being treated like a guest or an intern, your brain is trying to make sense of that dissonance by telling you, "Well, if everyone else is doing the job, maybe I’m not the mother." 

But that is a lie. 

You are the one who carried her. You are the one whose body she recognizes. You are the one who feels that "huge wave of love." That love is the only thing that matters, and it is the proof of your motherhood. 

And please, let me debunk the biggest myth of all: **Nobody "just knows" how to do this.** 

Everyone else you see—the women in your WhatsApp group, your mother, your Aai—they are all performing. They are all hiding their own insecurities, their own mistakes, and their own past moments of feeling like they were failing. The ones who look like they "just know" are often just the ones who have been allowed to make their own mistakes without an audience. 

You haven't been given the space to make your own mistakes. You haven't been given the space to figure out who *you* are as a mom, because you’re constantly being compared to an "expert." 

It is completely normal to feel like you can't breathe when you feel your identity slipping away. It’s a grief response. You are grieving the motherhood experience you thought you’d have. 

Since you asked me to just listen, I am holding that space for you. I am holding the truth that you *are* her mother, the only one she has, and that you are doing the hardest job in the world under the most difficult, crowded circumstances. 

I’m here. I’m listening. If you need to keep getting this out, keep going. What else is weighing on you?
